newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flynn criticises Britain on working directive.
newsitem.headline: Flynn criticises Britain on working directive.

text.p: EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn urged Britain on Tuesday to act urgently to implement the EU working time directive and criticised if for trying to hold treaty talks "ransom" over the law.

Speaking after Britain lost a court challenge to the directive, which sets an average maximum work week of 48 hours, Commissioner Padraig Flynn said he doubted Britain would succeed in its bid to get the EU treaty to nullify the rules.

"I fully expect that the UK will now take immediate and urgent steps to transpose the directive into national law so that employees in the UK can enjoy the protection which the directive provides," Flynn told a news conference.

British Prime Minister John Major said immediately after the ruling by the European Court of Justice that he would continue fighting the directive, 93/104/EC, which takes effect on November 23, within the EU's inter-governmental conference (IGC) on treaty reforms.
Trade and Industry Minister Ian Lang said in a statement Britain would obey the law while waiting for it to be changed.
"The United Kingdom failed to obtain what it wanted by the front door," Flynn said, referring to negotiations between EU ministers who adopted the directive in 1993.
"They failed by the back door in so far as the court action is concerned," he added. "And now they are attempting to break in through the IGC."

Britain challenged the EU directive on the grounds that it was improperly adopted as a health and safety measure requiring support from only a majority of EU countries under Article 118a of the EC Treaty. It charged the EU with attempting to slip in social legislation through the back door.
"They're now threatening to hold up the IGC to ransom if there is not a change in the treaty...Who is using the back door?" Flynn said.
He said he doubted that either the Commission or most EU countries would support Major's effort to change an existing EU law by amending the treaty.
"That would seem to me to be potentially very damaging to the legal order of the European Union," he said.

Flynn confirmed that the European Commission was examining the possibility of proposing that the working time directive be extended to workers that are now excluded -- a wide range of transport workers, seafarers and doctors in training.
He said that if the Commission decided to propose new rules after consulting labour and management representatives, it would use the same treaty article that Britain contested.
Flynn noted pointedly that Britain participated in the negotiations that produced the directive and won substantial concessions -- and that it abstained in the final vote rather than voting against.
For example, the rules allow national governments for a period of seven years to let workers put in more than 48 hours a week as long as it is done on a voluntary basis.

Britain won an opt-out from some workplace regulations in the Social Protocol of the EU's Maastricht Treaty. But Flynn said other other EU states had rejected the idea of adopting the working time directive under those provisions.
